title: Corporate Power Concentration — Public-Record Accountability Ledger
lead: Public institutional reporting across competition, wealth, labor, lobbying, climate, and digital infrastructure shows that concentrated corporate power now behaves as a governance problem rather than only an economic one.

retaliation_awareness: Preserve documentary chain-of-custody for every quoted source.
Separate adjudicated fact, corroborated reporting, allegation, and open question.
Log contradictions and unanswered questions without narrative smoothing.
Escalate named-party claims carrying legal or source-protection risk before publication.

editorial_sections.prefatory_note: This packet is a document-first investigative synthesis. It is structured for verification, challenge, legal review, and human editorial judgment.

entity_watchlist.name: Large platform firms
entity_watchlist.stated_position: Scale produces efficiency, innovation, and consumer benefit.
contradictions: Public competition and democracy research warns that scale can reduce contestability and harden governance dependence.

entity_watchlist.name: Private equity operators
entity_watchlist.stated_position: Operational discipline improves outcomes in essential sectors.
contradictions: Systematic review and public oversight reporting tie some rollup models to quality strain, cost pressure, and civic fragility.

entity_watchlist.name: Carbon majors
entity_watchlist.stated_position: Transition is underway and responsibility is diffuse across society.
contradictions: Carbon-accountability reporting continues to identify concentrated producer responsibility for a large share of industrial emissions.

open_questions: Which quiet chokepoints in public procurement produce the strongest form of vendor lock-in?
Which sectors most clearly convert wealth concentration into direct administrative leverage?
Where do current public data sources still under-measure ownership opacity or private-equity extraction?
